Silicate. Minerals containing silicon and oxygen, forming the largest and most abundant mineral class in Earth's crust. The characteristic structural unit is the silicate tetrahedron—a central silicon atom bonded to four oxygen atoms—which links in chains, sheets, or three-dimensional networks to create the vast diversity of silicate minerals. Over ninety-five percent of Earth's crust is composed of silicate minerals, making them foundational to geology, geochemistry, and most crustal rocks.

The silicate tetrahedron is the basic structural unit. Silicon atoms at Earth's temperature and pressure form strong tetrahedral bonds with oxygen, and these tetrahedra link to form chains, sheets, or frameworks depending on how many oxygens they share. Quartz, silicon dioxide, is the simplest silicate, a three-dimensional network of tetrahedra where every oxygen is shared between two silicon atoms. It is hard, resistant to weathering, and extremely common in igneous and sedimentary rocks.

Feldspars, the most abundant minerals in Earth's crust, making up approximately sixty percent of it, are framework silicates containing aluminum in addition to silicon and oxygen. They are the primary mineral in granite and many other igneous rocks. Olivine is an isolated-tetrahedron silicate with no shared oxygens, rich in iron and magnesium. It crystallizes early from cooling magma, forming the greenish mineral visible in basalt and peridotite.

Mica, including biotite and muscovite, are sheet silicates where tetrahedra form infinite two-dimensional sheets. They split easily along planes parallel to sheets, producing the characteristic flaky appearance. Amphiboles and pyroxenes are inosilicates—double- and single-chain silicates respectively—crystallizing in igneous rocks at high temperatures and forming elongated crystals. Silicate weathering, the chemical breakdown of silicate minerals by water and carbon dioxide, is a primary mechanism removing atmospheric carbon dioxide over geological time, regulating Earth's long-term climate.
